q: why do we have a blind spot
what causes the blind spot in the human eye
why do we still have a blind spot
a: The blind spot in human vision is caused by the structure of the retina. The retina contains light-sensitive cells (photoreceptors: rods and cones) that detect light and send signals to the brain via the optic nerve. Where the optic nerve exits the back of the eye, there are no photoreceptors — this creates a natural blind spot (called the optic disc) in each eye. The blind spot is located about 15 degrees to the outside of center vision. You dont normally notice your blind spot because your two eyes cover for each other (the blind spot of one eye is covered by the field of vision of the other eye) and because your brain fills in the gap using information from the surrounding visual field. You can find your blind spot with a simple test: draw a small dot and a small cross on a piece of paper about 6 inches apart. Close your right eye and look at the cross with your left eye. Move the paper toward or away from your face until the dot disappears. That is your blind spot. Evolution has not eliminated the blind spot because the structure of the retina evolved from inside-out (photoreceptors are at the back, behind blood vessels and nerve fibers). In cephalopods like octopuses, the retina evolved differently with photoreceptors on the surface, so they have no blind spot.
